cards.rueckseite:
- **Contiguous** (most common, ~40%): sinusitis, otitis media, dental abscess
- **Hematogenous**: lung infection, pulmonary AVF, cyanotic congenital heart disease, endocarditis, immunodeficiency
- **Penetrating**: trauma, neurosurgery, CSF leak

cards.text: Brain abscess pathogens: {{c1::Bacteroides}} and {{c2::Streptococcus milleri}} are found in > 50%; abscesses are frequently {{c3::polymicrobial}}.

zeilen: Thick ring enhancement on CT; slight resistance
T1 hypo / T2 hyper; no resistance

cards.vorderseite: Brain abscess: when are antibiotics alone sufficient?
cards.rueckseite:
- Cerebritis stage (symptoms < 2 weeks)
- Diameter < 3 cm
- Known organism
Typically **6–8 weeks IV** antibiotics.

- Significant mass effect / raised ICP
- No improvement after 4 weeks of antibiotics
- Proximity to the ventricle (risk of intraventricular rupture)
- Unknown pathogen
- Trapped foreign material
- Poor clinical condition
Options: stereotactic aspiration; craniotomy and excision if encapsulated or foreign body.

cards.text: Brain abscess outcome: mortality {{c1::10–20%}}, neurologic disability {{c2::~45%}}.

cards.rueckseite: 5× less common than brain abscess, more common than epidural abscess, M:F 3:1. Usually contiguous (sinus/ear) or after surgery. Associated brain abscess in **25%**. Can cause **cortical venous infarction**. Mortality 10–20%. **Surgical emergency** (burr holes early, usually craniotomy/debridement).

cards.text: Shunt infection: early infection risk {{c1::~5%}}; total incidence {{c2::10–15%}}; most common organism {{c3::coagulase-negative staphylococci / S. epidermidis (50–90%)}}.

cards.rueckseite:
**Two-stage:** remove the whole colonized shunt, place EVD, IV antibiotics until CSF is clear, then new shunt.
**One-stage:** complete exchange for a sterile shunt in one procedure, then IV antibiotics.
Antibiotics alone: poor success, only for patients unfit for surgery.
Rare immune-complex complication of chronic shunt infection, usually with **ventriculoatrial** shunts.
Antibiotics alone rarely curative. Usually **debridement and removal of the bone flap**, **6–12 weeks** of antibiotics, **cranioplasty after 3–6 months** once antibiotics are completed.
